7Zl_lAyUY4k.title: Supreme Court Just BLOCKED Missouri’s New Election Map
7Zl_lAyUY4k.description:
Missouri's congressional map fight just flipped again. The Eighth Circuit had ordered federal courts to require use of Missouri's newer 2025 congressional map—the same map used during the August primary. But the Supreme Court has now stayed those orders, leaving the 2022 map in place for the 2026 congressional election unless the Court later changes course. The Court emphasized that ballots using the old map had already been printed and mailed, absentee voting was underway, and switching maps again in the middle of an election could create “electoral chaos.” Supreme Court

I go through the Supreme Court's ruling and explain why the Eighth Circuit's constitutional argument didn't carry the day. The appeals court had concluded that using one congressional map for the primary and another for the general violated Article I, Section 2. The Supreme Court said its precedents have not established that rule and focused heavily on the timing of the federal intervention and the Purcell principle against federal courts changing election rules when voting is already underway. I also explain how Missouri managed to conduct its primary under one map while now preparing to conduct the general election under another.

Eddie Duran says that when Roger Fortson opened his apartment door holding a firearm, he believed he was about to be shot. Now the prosecutor gets to test that claim. It's whether Duran's perception of an imminent deadly-force threat was reasonable at the moment he fired. If it was reasonable, the shooting can be legally justified despite the tragic outcome. If it was unreasonable, Duran faces the manslaughter charge against him.

I explain the difference between controlling majority precedent and a dissent, why citing a dissent isn't inherently improper, and why I found the repeated pattern in this particular opinion so striking. I also break down what the Court actually decided about SAVE—and what remains unresolved because this is a stay proceeding rather than the final judgment in the case.

Roger Fortson was a law-abiding U.S. airman standing inside his own apartment with a firearm. Deputy Eddie Duran wasn't supposed to be at Fortson's apartment at all—he had been directed to the wrong unit while responding to what he believed was an escalating domestic-violence call. I explain why the mistaken apartment, the reported domestic violence, Duran's training, his position outside the doorway, Fortson's firearm, the roughly four-foot distance, and the fact that Fortson apparently never pointed the gun at Duran all matter when deciding whether that perception was reasonable.    1457_V2

2QtnYwcwTO8.description:
The Nolan Wells investigation is over for now, and the documents released afterward tell a remarkable story. The Jackson County grand jury unanimously returned a no true bill after issuing 132 subpoenas and hearing 43 witnesses. But the biggest revelation may be what District Attorney Angel McIlrath says happened behind the scenes: according to her statement, the Crump team advised her office on August 13 that they had discovered no evidence of a crime being committed against Nolan Wells. Yet she says public narratives portraying his death as racially motivated criminal violence continued afterward. 

I go through the prosecutor's correspondence and the actual grand-jury report, including what happened with Nolan's phone, what the family's independent medical examiner found, what GPS and security footage showed, and what the grand jury concluded about the people publicly accused of wrongdoing. The grand jury found no credible evidence that occupants of the three boats engaged in criminal conduct related to Wells's death and described allegations against them as the product of “public clamor and private malice.” I also explain why a grand jury exists not merely to indict people, but to protect people from being dragged into criminal court on unsupported accusations.

TZuDbjsf5wo.title: Federal Court Just OVERRULED Missouri Supreme Court’s Election Map
TZuDbjsf5wo.description:
WATCH FULL VIDEO: https://youtube.com/live/dlJo-Avqf34

Missouri already held its 2026 congressional primaries under one district map. Then the Missouri Supreme Court ordered the state to use a different map for the general election. That would leave large numbers of voters choosing among candidates in districts where they never participated in the primary. Now the Eighth Circuit has ruled that Missouri cannot switch congressional maps halfway through the same election process and ordered the federal district court to enter a permanent injunction requiring the 2025 map, subject to a short window for Supreme Court review.

I walk through the ruling and explain how Missouri ended up with state and federal courts issuing conflicting commands to the Secretary of State—including contempt proceedings after he followed a federal order. Most importantly, I break down the Eighth Circuit's constitutional reasoning: a congressional primary and general election are two stages of the same process, and the court concluded that moving voters between districts in the middle of that process violates Article I, Section 2.
